## 🌟 Summary
Release **v8.4.178** makes Platform training links more reliable and brings a broad set of fixes for model validation, tracking, exports, data loading, and training integrations. It also adds a cross-domain benchmark resource and expands Platform documentation.

## 📊 Key Changes
- **Reliable Platform training links (PR #26699):** Training now prints the model URL returned by the server, which knows the final owner, project, and model name. This avoids broken links when those details differ from the local training arguments; if the server provides no URL, no link is printed.
- **Broader model evaluation:** A new Ultralytics Benchmark page describes a fixed evaluation protocol across 37 real-world detection datasets, spanning areas such as medical imaging, retail, industry, and aerial imagery. The YOLO27 documentation also updates its reported performance figures and links to the benchmark.
- **Model and tracking compatibility:** YOLO-NAS receives fixes for loading by model name, prediction, validation, export, and ReID tracking. FastSAM prompts now persist across later images and video frames; SAM tracking preserves object IDs when masks are blank; and oriented-box tracking handles equivalent box representations more consistently.
- **More dependable validation and exports:** Validation now respects non-square input shapes recorded in static exports. Fixes also address TorchScript loading on Apple MPS, dynamic ONNX execution on MPS, and full-integer LiteRT/TensorFlow input handling.
- **Platform reporting improvements:** Validation curves now better match segmentation and pose results, and class labels stay aligned when validation data omits classes. Confusion-matrix logging is corrected for Comet and DVC, including cases where no matrix is available.
- **Training and workflow reliability:** TensorBoard writers close cleanly after training, FP32 optimizer momentum is retained in checkpoints, Ascend NPU training avoids an unsupported reduction, and Docker publishing skips overwriting tags with images built from newer commits.
- **Platform and documentation updates:** Platform guides document paid annotation and image-generation models, new Explore filters, and AI-assisted training diagnosis. Other fixes improve UTF-8 dataset and source-manifest reading, screenshot inputs, ZIP naming, and CLI error messages.

## 🎯 Purpose & Impact
- **Platform users** get working model links and clearer, more accurate training results.
- **Developers** benefit from more consistent behavior across model families, trackers, export formats, and hardware backends.
- **Teams managing experiments and data** get safer Docker releases, cleaner training teardown, and fewer failures caused by encoding, file naming, or configuration-directory issues.
- **Model evaluators** gain a broader reference for comparing performance beyond COCO; the benchmark results are documentation and evaluation resources, not a new model architecture in this release.

summary:
Prebuilt Newton WebAssembly simulations, their browser viewer, and exporter source for Isaac Lab documentation.

The documentation stages one reviewed, commit-named archive and verifies its SHA-256. This release is the permanent bundle container; updates add assets here without creating a new numbered release. Existing assets remain available for reproducible builds.

[Documentation update PR #8559](https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab/pull/8559) · [Review the gallery](https://maxkra15.github.io/isaaclab-browser-demos/lab/?v=grains-v1)

## Preview a bundle

Download the archive selected by `.github/actions/_lib/stage-browser-demos.sh`, extract it, and enter its top-level directory. Then run:

```bash
python -m http.server 8000 --directory site
```

Open `http://localhost:8000/interactive/`. The archive includes `exporters/`, scene and rebuild instructions, licenses, and `tools/publish.py`. Running the demos needs only a browser. Rebuilding physics requires the pinned internal Newton Web compiler and Emscripten.

## Publish an update

Reuse the `interactive-releases` publishing branch. Commit the reviewed site, create a commit-named archive and checksum, and upload both to this same release. Update the archive URL and SHA-256 together in the docs PR. Keep earlier assets and compatibility directories.

The current publishing branch is [available in the contributor fork](https://github.com/maxkra15/IsaacLab/tree/interactive-releases). Creating it in the official repository requires an administrator under the repository's branch-creation rule. Runtime bundles are hosted in this official release and served by Isaac Lab documentation.

summary: At a glance A new form of computing. Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption: making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency. Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029. Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. Spotlight: Microsoft research newsletter Microsoft Research Newsletter Stay connected to the research community at Microsoft. Subscribe today Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab), but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab), in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab), HyperNova (opens in new tab), NeutronNova (opens in new tab), Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab), in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab), Lasso (opens in new tab), Nebula (opens in new tab), and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second. More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab), a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab), which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust. If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab).
